Who is a Consumer
Consumer Protection Act, 2019
Definition: Under section 2(7) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, a consumer is a person who buys goods or hires or avails
services for consideration that has been paid, promised, partly paid and partly promised, or provided under a deferred-payment
system.

It includes an approved user of goods, but generally excludes a person who obtains goods for resale or for a commercial
purpose.

Important Exception: The Act generally excludes commercial-purpose purchases, but a person who buys goods exclusively to
earn livelihood by self-employment is treated differently under the statutory explanation.

The facts of each case matter.

Examples:
Buying a refrigerator for home use
Paying for a mobile recharge
Hiring a plumber for household repairs
Buying a sewing machine for personal self-employment may require fact-specific analysis
Not Normally Consumer Examples:
Buying goods for resale
Buying machinery for a large commercial enterprise
Hindi Expressions:
Main consumer hoon
Kya main is maamle mein consumer hoon?

Maine ghar ke liye saman kharida hai
Legal reference: Consumer Protection Act, 2019, Section 2(7)
Source: https://www.indiacode.nic.in/bitstream/123456789/18555/1/consumer_protection_act_2019.pdf
Keywords: consumer, section 2(7), commercial purpose, resale, self employment
Six Rights of Consumers
Consumer Rights
Rights:
Right to Safety: protection against goods and services hazardous to life and property
Right to Information: information about quality, quantity, potency, purity, standard and price
Right to Choice: access, wherever possible, to a variety of goods and services at competitive prices
Right to be Heard: consumer interests must receive due consideration at appropriate forums
Right to Seek Redressal: remedies against unfair or restrictive trade practices and exploitation
Right to Consumer Awareness: awareness of consumer rights and available remedies
Examples:
Safety: Unsafe electrical appliances should not be sold
Information: A packaged product should provide legally required particulars such as MRP, net quantity and expiry or best-before
information where applicable
Choice: A consumer should not be forced to buy an unwanted product as a condition of obtaining another product
Heard: A consumer can submit a grievance and supporting evidence to the seller, regulator or Consumer Commission
Redressal: A defective product may justify repair, replacement, refund or compensation depending on facts and the order
Awareness: Consumers should learn to check bills, terms, expiry dates, certifications and complaint channels
Plain Language: Consumer rights do not mean that every complaint automatically results in a refund.

The consumer normally
has to show the purchase or service relationship, the defect or deficiency, and the loss or unfair practice.

Legal reference: Consumer Protection Act, 2019, Section 2(9)

Source: https://consumeraffairs.gov.in/public/upload/admin/cmsfiles/whatsnews/New_Consumer_Protection_Act,_2019_-_FAQ_whatsnews.pdf,
https://www.consumerhelpline.gov.in/public/consumerrights
Keywords: six rights, right to safety, right to information, right to redressal, consumer awareness
Defect, Deficiency and Unfair Trade Practice
Consumer Protection Act, 2019
Defect: Section 2(10) defines defect as a fault, imperfection or shortcoming in the quality, quantity, potency, purity or standard
required by law, contract, express or implied representation, or the trader's claim in relation to goods or products.

Deficiency: Section 2(11) defines deficiency as a fault, imperfection, shortcoming or inadequacy in the quality, nature or manner
of performance required by law, contract or otherwise in relation to a service.

It includes negligent acts or omissions causing loss
or injury.

Unfair Trade Practice: Section 2(47) covers unfair or deceptive methods used to promote the sale or supply of goods or
services.

Examples include false claims about quality or quantity, misleading price representations, and refusing to take back
defective goods or refund the price within the promised or stipulated period.

Simple Difference:
Defect: Problem with a product, such as a phone that does not charge.

Deficiency: Problem with a service, such as a repair centre failing to perform the promised repair.

Unfair Trade Practice: Deception or unfair selling conduct, such as a fake discount or false quality claim.

Legal reference: Consumer Protection Act, 2019, Section 2(10), Section 2(11), Section 2(47)
Source: https://www.indiacode.nic.in/bitstream/123456789/15276/1/210422.pdf,
https://consumeraffairs.gov.in/public/upload/files/CP%20Act%202019_1732700731.pdf
Keywords: defect, deficiency, unfair trade practice, section 2(10), section 2(11), section 2(47)
Current Pecuniary Jurisdiction
Consumer Commissions
Basis: The current thresholds under the Consumer Protection (Consumer Disputes Redressal Commissions) Rules, 2021 are
based on the value of goods or services paid as consideration, not simply the compensation amount claimed.

District Commission: Up to and including ■50 lakh
State Commission: Above ■50 lakh and up to and including ■2 crore
National Commission: Above ■2 crore
Warning: Check the latest rules and applicable territorial jurisdiction before filing because statutory or regulatory changes may
occur.

Legal reference: Consumer Protection (Consumer Disputes Redressal Commissions) Rules, 2021, Consumer Protection Act, 2019, sections 34,
47 and 58
Source: https://consumeraffairs.nic.in/sites/default/files/232278.pdf, https://www.indiacode.nic.in/handle/123456789/15256?view_type=browse
Keywords: jurisdiction, ■50 lakh, ■2 crore, district commission, state commission, NCDRC
Where Can a Consumer Complaint Be Filed
Consumer Commissions
General Rule: A complaint may generally be filed before the Commission having territorial jurisdiction over the place where the
opposite party resides or carries on business, where the cause of action arose, or where the complainant resides or personally
works for gain, subject to the Act, rules and procedural requirements.

Practical Advice: For an online purchase, preserve the order address, seller details, payment record and delivery details.

Use
the official e-Jagriti or applicable Consumer Commission filing instructions to confirm the correct forum.

Warning: Jurisdiction questions can become fact-specific when there are multiple sellers, marketplaces, manufacturers,
branches or contractual clauses.

Practical Advice: For an online purchase, preserve the order address, seller details, payment record and delivery details.

Use
the official e-Jagriti or applicable Consumer Commission filing instructions to confirm the correct forum.

Warning: Jurisdiction questions can become fact-specific when there are multiple sellers, marketplaces, manufacturers,
branches or contractual clauses.

Legal reference: Consumer Protection Act, 2019 and Consumer Protection (Consumer Disputes Redressal Commissions) Rules, 2020, Section
34, Section 47, Section 58
Source: https://www.indiacode.nic.in/handle/123456789/15256?view_type=browse, https://consumeraffairs.gov.in/pages/e-jagriti
Keywords: territorial jurisdiction, place of residence, online purchase, cause of action, e-Jagriti
Two-Year Limitation for Consumer Complaints
Complaint Procedure
Rule: Under section 69 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, a Consumer Commission complaint should ordinarily be filed
within two years from the date on which the cause of action arose.

Delay: A delayed complaint may be admitted if the complainant satisfies the Commission that there was sufficient cause for the
delay and the Commission records reasons for condoning it.

Practical Advice: Do not wait for years while repeatedly contacting the seller.

Keep dated emails, complaint numbers, notices
and proof of follow-up, and obtain legal advice when limitation may be close.

Legal reference: Consumer Protection Act, 2019, Section 69
Source: https://www.indiacode.nic.in/handle/123456789/17038?view_type=browse&sam_handle=123456789/2510,
https://consumeraffairs.gov.in/public/upload/admin/cmsfiles/whatsnews/New_Consumer_Protection_Act,_2019_-_FAQ_whatsnews.pdf
Keywords: limitation, two years, section 69, delay condonation, cause of action
Step-by-Step Consumer Complaint Process
Complaint Procedure
Steps:
Identify the correct party or parties: seller, manufacturer, service provider, marketplace, insurer, bank or other responsible
entity.

Collect evidence: invoice, warranty, order page, payment proof, photographs, videos, emails, chats, call records, complaint
numbers, inspection reports and delivery records.

Send a clear written complaint to the trader or service provider.

State the facts, the remedy requested and a reasonable
response deadline.

Use the National Consumer Helpline for pre-litigation assistance where appropriate.

If unresolved, file before the appropriate Consumer Commission through the official e-Jagriti platform or the permitted offline
process.

State the facts chronologically, identify the defect, deficiency or unfair practice, list documents and specify the remedy sought.

Attend or participate in proceedings as directed.

Keep copies of filings, notices and orders.

If an order is passed and not complied with, seek appropriate enforcement or execution remedies under the applicable
procedure.

Evidence Examples:
Invoice or receipt
Screenshots of online order and product description
UPI or card transaction record
Defective product photographs or video
Warranty card and service reports
Emails and chat transcripts
Courier or delivery proof
Independent expert or laboratory report where technically necessary
Complaint Should Include:
Names and addresses of complainant and opposite party
Date and place of purchase or service
Amount paid
What was promised

What went wrong
Steps already taken
Loss or injury suffered
Relief requested
List of supporting documents
Important Note: A National Consumer Helpline grievance is a pre-litigation grievance mechanism; it is not the same as filing a
case before a Consumer Commission.
Legal reference: Consumer Protection Act, 2019, Section 35, Section 38, Section 39
Source: https://www.indiacode.nic.in/handle/123456789/15256?view_type=browse, https://consumeraffairs.gov.in/pages/e-jagriti,
https://consumerhelpline.gov.in/
Keywords: complaint process, consumer case, e-Jagriti, documents, legal notice, evidence
What Relief Can a Consumer Commission Grant
Remedies and Compensation
Possible Reliefs:
Removal of defects from goods
Replacement of goods
Refund of price paid, with interest where justified
Removal of deficiency in service
Compensation for loss or injury caused by negligence or deficiency
Discontinuance of unfair or restrictive trade practice
Withdrawal of hazardous goods from sale
Discontinuance of manufacture or provision of hazardous goods or services
Corrective advertisement for a misleading advertisement
Costs of litigation or proceedings where justified
Plain Language: The Commission chooses relief based on evidence, contract terms, the nature of the defect or deficiency,
actual loss and applicable law. A consumer should not assume that a full refund, replacement or punitive compensation is
automatic.
Legal reference: Consumer Protection Act, 2019, Section 39
Source: https://consumeraffairs.gov.in/public/upload/admin/cmsfiles/whatsnews/New_Consumer_Protection_Act,_2019_-_FAQ_whatsnews.pdf,
https://www.indiacode.nic.in/handle/123456789/15256?view_type=browse
Keywords: refund, replacement, compensation, repair, corrective advertisement, section 39
Consumer Mediation
Complaint Procedure
Meaning: Mediation is a settlement process in which a mediator helps the parties try to resolve the dispute. It is different from a
contested adjudication.
Practical Point: If a matter is referred to mediation, read the proposed settlement carefully. Do not sign a settlement that does
not clearly state payment amount, date, refund method, repair or replacement obligations, and consequences of default.
Warning: Mediation is not suitable for every dispute, especially where urgent safety, fraud, criminal conduct or a strong need for
an authoritative finding is involved.
Legal reference: Consumer Protection Act, 2019, Section 2(25), Sections 74 to 81
Source: https://www.indiacode.nic.in/bitstream/123456789/18555/1/consumer_protection_act_2019.pdf
Keywords: mediation, settlement, consumer mediator, sections 74 to 81
e-Jagriti and Online Consumer Commission Filing
Digital Complaint Filing

Purpose: e-Jagriti is the Department of Consumer Affairs platform and resource system for consumer-related digital services and
Consumer Commission case filing.
Steps:
Open the official e-Jagriti information or filing platform.
Create an account using the required identity and contact details.
Select the appropriate Consumer Commission and complaint type.
Enter parties, facts, reliefs and case value.
Upload readable documents and pay any applicable fee shown by the official portal.
Save the filing acknowledgement, diary or case number and monitor notices.
Warning: Portal names, links, filing workflows and technical requirements can change. Use the current official Department of
Consumer Affairs or Consumer Commission portal rather than unofficial websites.
Source: https://consumeraffairs.gov.in/pages/e-jagriti, https://consumeraffairs.gov.in/pages/consumer-protection-unit-consumer-commission,
https://edaakhil.nic.in/edaakhil/
Keywords: e-Jagriti, e-Daakhil, online consumer case, digital filing, consumer commission portal
National Consumer Helpline
Authorities
Role: The National Consumer Helpline is a Department of Consumer Affairs pre-litigation grievance mechanism. It can facilitate
communication with participating companies and help consumers understand possible channels, but it does not replace a
Consumer Commission, regulator, police investigation or court.
Phone Numbers:
1915
1800 11 4000
Timings: 8:00 AM to 8:00 PM on all days except national holidays, according to the official contact page
Channels:
Web portal
NCH consumer app
UMANG
WhatsApp: 8800001915
SMS: 8800001915
Email: nch-ca@gov.in
Documents:
Invoice or order number
Payment proof
Written communication with seller
Photographs or screenshots
Warranty or policy documents
Practical Advice: Ask for and preserve the docket number. If the grievance remains unresolved, consider the relevant regulator,
police or Consumer Commission rather than repeatedly opening identical tickets.
Source: https://consumerhelpline.gov.in/about-portal.php, https://consumerhelpline.gov.in/public/contact,
https://consumeraffairs.gov.in/pages/nch
Keywords: NCH, 1915, 1800 11 4000, INGRAM, consumer helpline, docket number
Defective Product: Repair, Replacement or Refund
Products and Warranties
Process:
Stop using a product that may be unsafe.
Photograph the product, serial number, packaging, defect and any resulting damage.

Contact the seller and manufacturer or authorised service centre in writing.

Quote the invoice, warranty and promised specifications.

Ask clearly for repair, replacement or refund and state a response deadline.

Keep the product available for inspection and do not destroy or alter evidence.

If unresolved, use NCH or file before the Consumer Commission.

Legal Position: A Consumer Commission may order removal of defects, replacement, refund, compensation or other relief under
section 39.

The appropriate remedy depends on the evidence, warranty terms, seriousness of the defect, repair history and loss
caused.

Warranty Note: A warranty is a contractual promise with stated terms and duration.

It does not automatically guarantee
replacement of the entire product or a refund in every case.

Read exclusions, service conditions and proof-of-purchase
requirements.

Sample Request: The product delivered on [date] does not match the promised specification and has the following defect:
[facts].

I request [repair/replacement/refund] under the warranty and applicable consumer law.

Please respond in writing by
[date].

Legal reference: Consumer Protection Act, 2019, Section 2(10), Section 2(20), Section 2(47), Section 39
Source: https://consumeraffairs.gov.in/public/upload/files/CP%20Act%202019_1732700731.pdf,
https://www.indiacode.nic.in/handle/123456789/15256?view_type=browse
Keywords: defective product, warranty, repair, replacement, refund, service centre
Warranty, Guarantee and Repair Rights
Products and Warranties
Warranty: A warranty is generally a written promise regarding repair, replacement, parts or service for a stated period and under
specified conditions.

Guarantee: A guarantee may be a stronger promise, but its legal effect depends on the wording, contract, product representation
and applicable law.

Consumer Checklist:
Confirm whether the promise is from the manufacturer, seller or service provider.

Check duration, exclusions, accidental-damage conditions and inspection requirements.

Keep the invoice, warranty card, serial number and service job sheets.

Ask for a written reason if a claim is rejected.

Do not accept an oral refusal as the final position; request email or job-sheet remarks.

Important Case Awareness: Frequent repairs alone may not prove a manufacturing defect, and a vehicle warranty may entitle
the consumer only to replacement of defective parts under its terms rather than automatic replacement of the entire vehicle or
refund.

The result depends on facts and evidence.

Source: https://consumeraffairs.gov.in/public/upload/files/E-digest%20of%20Judgments_1767084682.pdf,
https://consumeraffairs.gov.in/public/upload/files/CP%20Act%202019_1732700731.pdf
Keywords: warranty, guarantee, repair rights, manufacturing defect, service job sheet
Online Shopping, Marketplace and E-Commerce Rights
Digital/E-Commerce
Common Problems:
Non-delivery after payment
Wrong, fake, used or damaged product
Product materially different from listing
Seller refusing return or refund
Cancellation without refund
Extra charges at checkout
Unclear seller identity or grievance contact
Fake reviews or manipulated ratings

Practical Steps:
Save the product page, seller details, order confirmation, invoice, payment record and delivery-unboxing video where possible.
Complain through the platform and separately identify the seller, marketplace and manufacturer where relevant.
Use the platform grievance officer details displayed on the website or app.
Ask for a written explanation and refund or replacement.
Escalate to NCH, CCPA or Consumer Commission as appropriate.
Legal Rule: The Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020 require e-commerce entities to maintain a grievance redressal
mechanism and appoint a grievance officer whose name and contact details must be displayed. The grievance officer should
acknowledge a consumer complaint within 48 hours and redress it within one month.
Marketplace Note: A marketplace and a seller may have different legal roles. Identify all relevant parties from the invoice, listing
and terms instead of assuming that only the app is responsible.
Legal reference: Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020
Source: https://consumeraffairs.gov.in/public/upload/files/E%20commerce%20rules_1732703966.pdf,
https://consumeraffairs.gov.in/pages/consumer-protection-acts
Keywords: e-commerce, marketplace, online shopping, non delivery, wrong product, grievance officer, 48 hours, one month
Online Non-Delivery
Problem: Consumer paid online but the product was never delivered.
Payment receipt
Order confirmation email
Order page and promised delivery date
Seller and platform details
Customer-care complaint number
Ask the platform and seller for delivery or full refund in writing.
Use the e-commerce grievance officer and NCH.
If unresolved, file a Consumer Commission complaint for deficiency in service and appropriate refund or compensation.
Hindi Expression: Maine paisa diya, saman nahi aaya
Legal reference: Consumer Protection Act, 2019; Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020
Source: https://consumeraffairs.gov.in/public/upload/files/E%20commerce%20rules_1732703966.pdf,
https://www.indiacode.nic.in/bitstream/123456789/15276/1/210422.pdf
Keywords: non delivery, online order, refund, deficiency of service
Wrong, Fake or Damaged Product Delivery
Problem: The consumer ordered one product but received another product, a counterfeit product or a damaged product.
Product listing screenshot
Invoice
Package label and barcode
Unboxing video or delivery photographs
Return request and rejection message
Do not use the product if it may be unsafe or counterfeit.
Raise return or replacement request immediately.

Preserve packaging and courier labels.
Ask for refund including eligible delivery charges.
Escalate to platform grievance officer, NCH, CCPA or Consumer Commission.
Hindi Expression: Order mobile kiya tha, soap mila
Legal reference: Consumer Protection Act, 2019; Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020
Source: https://consumeraffairs.gov.in/public/upload/files/CP%20Act%202019_1732700731.pdf,
https://consumeraffairs.gov.in/public/upload/files/E%20commerce%20rules_1732703966.pdf
Keywords: wrong product, counterfeit, damaged delivery, return, refund
Dark Patterns and Deceptive Interfaces
Digital/E-Commerce
Meaning: A dark pattern is a user-interface design or practice that deceives, manipulates or substantially impairs a consumer's
ability to make a free and informed choice.
Official Examples:
False urgency
Basket sneaking
Confirm shaming
Forced action
Subscription trap
Interface interference
Bait and switch
Drip pricing
Disguised advertisements
Nagging
Trick wording
SaaS billing
Rogue malware
Consumer Actions:
Take screenshots before completing payment.
Record the advertised price and final checkout price.
Look for pre-ticked add-ons, automatic renewals and hidden cancellation steps.
Cancel unwanted subscriptions and ask for refund promptly.
Report the practice to the platform, NCH or CCPA and preserve evidence.
Remedy: A consumer may pursue refund or other relief under applicable consumer law. The CCPA may investigate and act
against prohibited practices under its statutory powers.
Legal reference: Guidelines for Prevention and Regulation of Dark Patterns, 2023
Source: https://consumeraffairs.nic.in/sites/default/files/file-uploads/latestnews/central-consumer-protection-authority-dark-patterns-guidelines-wa
termark-1565354.pdf
Keywords: dark patterns, basket sneaking, subscription trap, drip pricing, false urgency, CCPA
Misleading Advertisements and Endorsements
Advertising and CCPA
Examples:
False claim about quality, performance, purity or safety
Claiming a product is free when mandatory charges are hidden
Showing a fake or inflated reference price
Using an unsubstantiated health, education, investment or employment claim
Influencer endorsement without disclosing a material commercial connection

Advertisement that omits material information likely to mislead consumers
Consumer Actions:
Save the advertisement URL, date, screenshots, video and transaction record.
Complain to the seller or advertiser.
Report to CCPA or NCH.
Seek appropriate refund or compensation before the Consumer Commission where the advertisement caused a purchase or
loss.
Endorsement Rule: The 2022 guidelines require due diligence by endorsers. An endorsement should reflect the genuine and
reasonably current opinion of the endorser, be based on adequate information or experience, not be deceptive, and disclose a
material connection that the audience would not reasonably expect.
Legal reference: Guidelines for Prevention of Misleading Advertisements and Endorsements for Misleading Advertisements, 2022
Source: https://consumeraffairs.nic.in/regulations-made-under-consumer-protection-act-2019, https://consumeraffairs.nic.in/sites/default/files/Con
sumer%20Protection%20Act,%202019%20protects%20consumers%20involved%20in%20online%20transactions%20English.pdf
Keywords: misleading advertisement, endorsement, influencer, CCPA, fake claim, fake discount
Fake or Inflated Discount
Problem: A seller increases the reference price and then displays a large discount, or advertises a discount that is not available
at checkout.
Advertisement screenshot
Checkout screenshot
Invoice
Price history from reliable records
Date and time of the offer
Ask the seller to honour the displayed offer or refund the overcharge where appropriate.
Report misleading advertisement or deceptive pricing to CCPA or NCH.
File a Consumer Commission complaint if a purchase and loss occurred.
Hindi Expression: Discount jhootha hai
Legal reference: Consumer Protection Act, 2019; Misleading Advertisements and Endorsements Guidelines, 2022, Section 2(47), Section 18
Source: https://consumeraffairs.nic.in/sites/default/files/Consumer%20Protection%20Act,%202019%20protects%20consumers%20involved%20i
n%20online%20transactions%20English.pdf, https://consumeraffairs.nic.in/regulations-made-under-consumer-protection-act-2019
Keywords: fake discount, inflated price, misleading advertisement, drip pricing
Subscription Trap and Auto-Renewal
Problem: A consumer unknowingly enrolled in an auto-renewing subscription or found cancellation much harder than sign-up.
Subscription screen
Terms and conditions
Email or SMS confirmation
Bank or card statement
Cancellation attempt screenshots
Cancel the subscription through the provider and payment instrument.
Ask for confirmation that auto-renewal has stopped.
Demand refund for an unauthorised or inadequately disclosed charge.

Complain to the platform, NCH or CCPA and consider a Consumer Commission complaint if money was lost.
Safety Note: Do not share OTP, UPI PIN, card PIN or remote-access credentials while seeking a refund.
Legal reference: Guidelines for Prevention and Regulation of Dark Patterns, 2023
Source: https://consumeraffairs.nic.in/sites/default/files/file-uploads/latestnews/central-consumer-protection-authority-dark-patterns-guidelines-wa
termark-1565354.pdf
Keywords: subscription trap, auto renewal, recurring payment, refund, dark pattern
Hidden Charges and Drip Pricing
Problem: Extra charges appear only at the final checkout stage or are not clearly disclosed before payment.
Initial price screenshot
Cart and checkout screenshots
Invoice
Terms displayed at the time of purchase
Ask for reversal of undisclosed charges.
Use the platform grievance mechanism and NCH.
Report suspected drip pricing or unfair practice to CCPA.
Claim refund or compensation before the Consumer Commission if loss occurred.
Legal reference: Consumer Protection Act, 2019; Guidelines for Prevention and Regulation of Dark Patterns, 2023
Source: https://consumeraffairs.nic.in/sites/default/files/file-uploads/latestnews/central-consumer-protection-authority-dark-patterns-guidelines-wa
termark-1565354.pdf, https://www.indiacode.nic.in/bitstream/123456789/15276/1/210422.pdf
Keywords: hidden charges, drip pricing, checkout, unfair trade practice
Banking Complaints and Escalation
Sector-Specific
Problems:
Unexplained charges
Failed UPI transactions
Unauthorised electronic transactions
Cash not received but account debited
Wrong interest or loan charges
Unfair recovery conduct
Credit-card billing dispute
Failure to close account or issue documents
First Step: Complain to the bank, regulated entity, card issuer or payment service provider through its official grievance channel.
Obtain a complaint number.
Escalation: If the regulated entity rejects the complaint, does not reply within 30 days, or the response is unsatisfactory, use the
RBI Complaint Management System under the Integrated Ombudsman Scheme where the entity and matter are covered.
Bank statement
Transaction ID or UTR
ATM slip
SMS or email alert
Screenshots
Written complaint and bank response

Remedy Note: Consumer Commission remedies and RBI regulatory grievance mechanisms may overlap in some situations, but
the correct forum depends on the entity, transaction and relief sought.

Fraud should also be reported to police or the cybercrime
system.

Source: https://www.rbi.org.in/CommonPerson/english/Scripts/PressReleases.aspx?Id=3340,
https://www.rbi.org.in/commonperson/english/scripts/FAQs.aspx?Id=3407, https://cms.rbi.org.in/
Keywords: banking complaint, RBI Ombudsman, CMS, bank charges, grievance officer, 30 days
RBI Integrated Ombudsman Scheme
Banking and Financial Services
Eligibility Sequence:
First complain in writing to the concerned bank, NBFC or covered payment system participant.

Wait for the entity's reply or the expiry of 30 days if there is no reply.

If the reply is unsatisfactory or absent, file through the RBI Complaint Management System, subject to the Scheme's coverage
and exclusions.

Channels:
Online: https://cms.rbi.org.in/
Contact Centre: 14448, with hours and language availability as stated by RBI
Email or physical filing through the RBI Centralised Receipt and Processing Centre, as specified by RBI
Documents:
Original complaint to the regulated entity

Everyday Consumer Protection Checklist
Awareness
Before Purchase:
Compare the total price, including delivery, taxes, convenience fees and recurring charges.
Check seller identity, address, contact details, return policy and warranty.
Verify relevant BIS mark, HUID, licence or registration where applicable.
Be cautious of urgent countdowns, unrealistic discounts and guaranteed results.

At Purchase:
Ask for a proper invoice or receipt.

Check MRP, net quantity, manufacturing or packing date, expiry or best-before date and product condition.

Confirm model, colour, specification, warranty and promised delivery date.

Use secure payment methods and never share OTP, PIN or passwords.

After Purchase:
Keep invoices, screenshots, payment records and correspondence.

Report defects quickly and in writing.

Record complaint numbers and deadlines.

Do not discard packaging where authenticity, damage or return is disputed.

Track the two-year Consumer Commission limitation period.

Which Authority Should I Approach
Authorities and Escalation
General Consumer Grievance: Seller or service provider → National Consumer Helpline → Consumer Commission through
official e-Jagriti or applicable filing process.

Bank Or Nbfc: Regulated entity grievance channel → RBI Complaint Management System or Ombudsman if covered and
preconditions are met.

Upi Or Payment Fraud: Bank or payment provider immediately → 1930 and cybercrime.gov.in → RBI or other appropriate
regulator where applicable.

Insurance: Insurer grievance officer → IRDAI Bima Bharosa → Insurance Ombudsman or Consumer Commission where eligible.

Telecom: Telecom complaint centre → provider's Appellate Authority, commonly through 198 → other appropriate remedy.

Food: Seller or manufacturer → FSSAI Food Safety Connect or State Food Safety authority → NCH or Consumer Commission
for consumer relief.

Bis Or Hallmark: Seller or jeweller → BIS Care or BIS complaint channel → NCH or Consumer Commission for refund or
compensation.

Securities: Broker or regulated intermediary → exchange or depository grievance route where applicable → SEBI SCORES.

Real Estate: Promoter or agent → State RERA Authority or adjudicating officer → appeal or other consumer remedy as legally
appropriate.

Weights And Measures: Seller → State Legal Metrology authority → NCH or Consumer Commission for consumer relief.

Criminal Conduct: Police, emergency service or cybercrime authorities; regulatory and consumer complaints do not replace
criminal reporting.

Employment Dispute Is Usually Not a Consumer Complaint
Scope Boundaries
Problem: An employer withholds salary, benefits or employment dues.
Correct Route: This is ordinarily an employment or labour dispute, not a Consumer Commission matter, because an employee
generally does not hire the employer's service as a consumer.
Approach the labour department, labour commissioner, appropriate tribunal or court.
Use the employment contract, salary slips, attendance records and written demand.
Seek legal advice for limitation and forum selection.
Warning: Do not automatically file an employment dispute before a Consumer Commission. The correct forum depends on the
employment relationship and applicable labour law.
Source: https://labour.gov.in/
Keywords: employment, salary, labour dispute, scope boundary, labour commissioner

Real Estate and Scope
Problem: A person is cheated in a land purchase, faces title problems or does not receive promised possession.

AI Legal Safety Rules
AI/Legal Safety
Rules:
Provide general legal awareness, not personalised legal representation.
Do not promise a result, refund, compensation or guaranteed success.
Distinguish a regulator complaint, NCH grievance, Consumer Commission case, civil proceeding and criminal complaint.
Cite the applicable Act, section, rule, authority and official source where available.
State when a rule is fact-specific, subject to exclusions or likely to change.
For urgent safety, medical injury, criminal fraud, limitation expiry, large financial loss or property title disputes, encourage timely
professional advice.
Never ask a consumer to share OTP, UPI PIN, card PIN, password or remote-access details.
Use only verified official URLs and do not invent complaint numbers, deadlines or legal provisions.
